# Plant breeding — methods and examples

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Plant breeding — methods and examples** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Plant breeding — methods and examples

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

**Plant breeding** is the purposeful genetic improvement of crop plants: cross parents carrying desirable traits, select the best offspring over generations, and release a stable, superior variety. The classic steps: collection of germplasm → hybridisation → selection → testing → release. Success stories: high-yielding wheat and rice of the Green Revolution, and fortified crops like iron-rich spinach varieties.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the five steps of classical plant breeding (study in this order)**

| Step | Stage | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Germplasm collection | Gather all available wild relatives, landraces and improved varieties — the raw material |
| 2 | Hybridisation | Cross selected parents carrying complementary traits (emasculation + bagging for controlled pollination) |
| 3 | Selection | Over generations, keep only the progeny with the best combination of traits |
| 4 | Testing and evaluation | Grow candidates in multi-location field trials vs the best existing varieties |
| 5 | Release and distribution | Officially released variety; seed multiplied and sold to farmers |

**Breeding achievements — the classic examples**

| Achievement | Crop / organism | What was bred for |
|---|---|---|
| Green Revolution wheat | Sonora 64, Lerma Rojo (Norman Borlaug era) | Semi-dwarf, high-yield, fertiliser-responsive |
| Green Revolution rice | IR-8 and derivatives | High yield, short straw, wide adaptability |
| Fortified spinach | Iron-enriched spinach varieties | Higher iron content to fight anaemia |
| Hybrid maize and sorghum | Single-cross hybrids | Vigour (heterosis) and uniformity |
| Disease resistance | Various crops vs rust, blight | Resistance genes from wild relatives |

## 5. Worked examples and applications

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — the semi-dwarf wheat that fed billions.** Borlaug's team crossed a Japanese dwarf wheat (carrying height-reducing genes) with high-yielding American varieties. Selection over generations fixed semi-dwarf stature: short, stiff straw that stands up under heavy grain and fertiliser without lodging (falling over). Released as Sonora 64 and Lerma Rojo, adapted to India and Pakistan, yields doubled — the Green Revolution. One trait (short straw) unlocked the whole yield package.

(4) What is biofortification — give an example (iron-fortified spinach). (5) Why is germplasm collection step 1 and not an afterthought?

mcqs.explanation: Every NEB rule has a scope (e.g. a specific range, temperature, or sign convention); stating the condition earns full marks.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Six-step classical protocol: collection of variability → evaluation and selection of parents → cross-hybridisation → selection of superior recombinants → testing/release (multi-year field trials) — the ordered list IS the answer.
Trick 2: Examples: semi-dwarf wheat (Norman Borlaug, Sonalika/Kalyan Sona), rice (Jaya, IR-8), sugarcane (Saccharum × Saccharum barbari), millets hybrid — quote two.
Trick 3: Fortification breeding: Atlas 66 wheat (high protein) and iron-fortified spinach varieties — the nutrition angle.
Trick 4: Mutation breeding: gamma rays/chemicals create variation (mohan rice variety); polyploidy via colchicine — the non-conventional methods.
